title: Setup process, mulligan, and deck legality (101-118, 103.2, 825)
prompt: Walk the Setup Process end to end (110-118) and the deckbuilding constraints that gate it (101-103, 825 Unique). Contrasts to test: a legal 40-card Main Deck with the Chosen Champion separated into the Champion Zone (112, 108.3) versus a deck where the Chosen Champion was left in the Main Deck; a Champion Legend in the Legend Zone (111) versus none; 3 copies of a named card allowed (103.2.b) versus a 4th rejected; 3 Signature cards sharing the Legend's Champion Tag allowed (103.2.d) versus a Signature card whose Champion Tag does not match the Legend; a Unique card interacting with the Signature allowance (825.3.b) — does the engine let a deck hold three Unique-Signature copies where the rules permit combinations, and does it reject the same set when Unique is printed on a non-Signature card? Then the mulligan itself (116-117): each player draws 4, mulligans in turn order, and the harness must surface a per-seat mulligan Decision naming the exact hand — assert that the mulliganed cards go back and are reshuffled before the redraw, that a second mulligan is not offered, and that the non-turn player's mulligan Decision is offered to seat 2 and not seat 1. Also assert battlefield selection (113, 485.5): each player picks one of three battlefields and the other two are set aside where card effects cannot reach them, and that the first-turn adjustment (485.7 — the player going second channels an extra rune during their first Channel Phase) actually fires exactly once. Every facet that is silently auto-resolved instead of prompted is a bug worth recording.

title: Mode variables and multiplayer-safe assumptions that must hold in 1v1 (481-489, 194, 462)
prompt: The engine is a 2-player engine, but the rules are written for FFA3/FFA4/2v2 as well (481-489), and several rules are phrased as multiplayer guards that must still behave correctly at 2 players. Probe the mode variables of 1v1 Duel (485): Victory Score 8 (483.3, 194.3), Battlefield Count 2 (485.4, 172), first-turn extra channel (485.7). Then hunt for places where a multiplayer-flavored rule was implemented as a no-op or was hardcoded wrong: 'next player in turn order' for priority passing (339.2) must be the single opponent and must round-trip; 'each opponent' / 'each other player' effects must hit exactly one player and count as one, not zero and not two; 462 (combat only between exactly two players) and 462.1-462.3 must be trivially satisfied rather than crash a battlefield with three-sided presence that cannot occur; 732 (XP is not shared between allies) must not accidentally pool XP; 315.2.b.3 (teammate-controlled battlefields do not Hold for the turn player) must not grant the opponent a hold. Also test tie-breaking at 194.2.a: both players at or above the Victory Score in the same Cleanup — the player with MORE points wins, and if truly tied nobody wins yet; assert the game does not end and the Cleanup repeats. Multi-card setup a judge gets asked about: a symmetric 'each player gains a point' effect resolving while both players sit at 7 — surface the exact win Decision or lack of one. Prefer facets where a 2-player shortcut would look right in casual play but is provably wrong.

title: Awaken Phase, Beginning Step, and the Hold scoring step (315.1, 315.2)
prompt: The Start of Turn is three rigid phases and the engine must not blur them (314-315). Awaken (315.1.b): the turn player readies ALL game objects they control that are able to be readied — test that this covers units at battlefields, non-unit gear at base, runes, and legends, but NOT objects controlled by the opponent, and NOT an object under a 'does not ready during your Awaken Phase' style restriction (415.1.b/415.3.a plus 054 can't-beats-can). Beginning Step (315.2.a.1): 'at the start of Beginning Phase' triggers fire here — set up two such triggers on the same side and assert an order Decision (383.3.d), and one on each side to assert turn-order batching. Scoring Step (315.2.b.2): the turn player Holds all battlefields they Control, which is a Score (469.2) and therefore fires 'when you score / when I hold' abilities at each battlefield (471.2) — contrast holding TWO battlefields (two separate scores, two point gains, two ability triggers, order chosen by the turn player) against holding a battlefield already scored this turn via a Conquer in the same turn cycle (470: once per battlefield per turn, so no second point). Also test control established but no unit present at the moment of the Scoring Step (323.6 loses control in an Open State cleanup) versus a lone exhausted unit still holding. The harness should surface: a ready-list, a start-of-Beginning trigger order Decision, and a per-battlefield score event with the point delta and the battlefield id.

title: Channel Phase and Draw Phase, including empty decks (315.3, 315.4, 430, 413, 431)
prompt: Channel Phase (315.3.b): the turn player channels 2 runes from the Rune Deck, readied by default (430.2.a), and channels as many as possible if fewer than 2 remain (315.3.b.1, 430.3) — contrast a Rune Deck with 5, with exactly 1, and with 0, asserting the count actually channeled and that no Burn Out is triggered by an empty RUNE deck (431.1 applies to the Main Deck). Test an effect that channels exhausted, and an effect that channels an additional rune (485.7 for the player going second) — does the extra rune stack with the base 2 and does it fire only on that player's FIRST turn? Draw Phase (315.4.b): the turn player draws 1; with an empty Main Deck they Burn Out and then STILL draw 1 (315.4.b.2, 413.4) — assert the exact sequence: draw as many as possible, Burn Out (431.2 shuffle trash into deck, opponent gains a point), then complete the draw, and assert the point actually landed on the OPPONENT. Then the pathological case a judge gets asked about: empty Main Deck AND empty trash, so the deck stays empty (431.3) — the player burns out repeatedly and the opponent accrues points until the Victory Score, with the win checked at the following Cleanup (431.3.c, 323.1, 472). Also test a 'skip your draw phase' style replacement (443 Skip) versus a 'draw an additional card' modifier, and whether at-start-of-phase triggers still fire on a skipped phase. Surface the Burn Out event and the resulting point total per seat.

title: Ending Step, Expiration Step, and the FEPR re-loop (317, 318, 816)
prompt: The Ending Phase has two steps and an explicit loop that engines routinely flatten (317). Ending Step (317.1.a): 'at the end of the turn' effects take place — put two on one side and one on the other and assert the order Decision plus turn-order batching. Expiration Step (317.2): an Ending Special Cleanup with three inserted steps in a fixed order — 3c heal all units, 3d all 'this turn' effects expire simultaneously, 3e each player's rune pool empties (317.2.b-d). Test the yes/no contrasts a judge is asked: a unit at 3 damage with a 'gets +2 might this turn' buff — it heals BEFORE the this-turn buff expires, so it survives; a unit whose might is only above its marked damage because of a this-turn pump — because 3c precedes 3d, it must NOT die at end of turn; a Temporary unit (816) killed during 3d and its Deathknell (808) — does the death happen inside the expiration and does the resulting trigger force the re-loop? 317.2.f is the key mechanism: if any items underwent the FEPR process, return to the START of the Expiration Step — so a Deathknell that resolves during expiration causes a SECOND heal and a SECOND 'this turn' expiry pass; assert the engine loops rather than falling through to 317.3. Also assert stunned units lose Stunned at 3d (423.1.a.2) and that unspent energy and power are gone before the next player's turn (167). Surface: the ordered list of expiration sub-steps executed, and the loop count.

title: Cleanup triggers, the ten ordered Cleanup tasks, and cascading Cleanups (318-324)
prompt: Cleanup is the engine's most load-bearing loop and 323 fixes an exact ten-task order. Test that a Cleanup becomes outstanding for each listed cause (319.1-319.8): state transitions, phase transitions, a pending item added to the chain, an item finalized, an item leaving the chain, objects entering/leaving the board, status changes, and a completed Move — pick a scenario per cause and assert exactly one Cleanup (not zero, not two). Then walk 323 order with a setup that makes the order observable: a unit with lethal damage that also has Deathknell (323.4 gathers those triggers at 3a, then 323.5 kills at 3b), a battlefield the controller no longer occupies (323.6, only in an Open State), an unattached non-unit gear left at a battlefield (323.7 recall), Contested applied and then removed (323.8-323.11), and a Showdown or Combat staged at the end (323.12-323.14). Yes/no contrasts: win check at 323.1 happens FIRST, before deaths are processed — so a player who crosses the Victory Score wins even though a lethal-damaged unit of theirs has not yet died; deaths during a Cleanup queue ANOTHER Cleanup after this one (322), not a nested one; 320 and 321 forbid finalizing/resolving during a Cleanup and forbid a Cleanup during resolution — build a scenario where a resolving spell kills two units and assert no Cleanup interleaves mid-resolution. Surface the ordered task log for one Cleanup and the number of cascaded Cleanups.

title: Finalize / Execute / Pass / Resolve mechanics and the chain zone (327-340)
prompt: Drill the raw FEPR loop rather than any card's text (332-340). Finalize (337.1): the controller of the OLDEST Pending item finalizes first — build a chain where seat 1 has a pending spell and a seat-2 trigger becomes pending after it, and assert the finalize order is by age, not by controller or by board scan. 337.2 is the sharp one: a finalized Unit, Gear, or resource-Adding ability does NOT linger and does not pass priority — assert that playing a unit while a spell sits finalized does not give the opponent a window on the unit itself, while a spell does (359.3.c). 337.3/337.4: if items remain pending, return to Finalize; only when none remain does the controller of the newest item get priority. Pass (339.1): all players pass IN SEQUENCE without adding items before anything resolves — assert that a player who adds an item resets the pass chain and that priority goes to the next player in turn order (339.2). Resolve (340.1): only the NEWEST finalized item resolves, then 340.3/340.4 decide whether we return to Finalize or hand priority to the controller of the new newest item — test LIFO with three items where order changes the outcome (a buff, a damage spell that checks might, a counter). Also assert 328/330: the chain zone exists only while an item is on it, and 336.1 items becoming pending mid-FEPR join the current pass. Surface the chain contents as an ordered list at every priority window and the seat holding priority.

title: Priority versus Focus — who may act, and when (311-313, 342-348)
prompt: Priority and Focus are distinct permissions and conflating them is a classic engine bug (311-313). Assert: at most one player has each (312, 313); a player who gains Focus also gains Priority (313.2); a player who PASSES Priority retains Focus (313.3); a player with Focus but not Priority may not take discretionary actions (313.4); in a Neutral State no player has Focus at all (313.5). Build the canonical judge scenario: seat 2 moves into seat 1's battlefield, Contested is applied, a Showdown opens and the CONTESTER gains Focus (345) — not the turn player. Seat 2 (Focus) plays a spell; both players get priority windows on that chain; when the chain empties and the turn returns to an Open State during the Showdown, Focus passes to the next player (346) — except when the chain opened from a triggered ability being added, where Focus does NOT pass (346.1); test both branches with a triggered-ability-opened chain versus a played-spell-opened chain. Also test what the non-Focus player may legally do during a Showdown: only Reaction-tagged cards and abilities (813), never a plain sorcery-speed spell (155, 358.4) — assert seat.can is false and that attempting it throws. Contrast a turn player who tries to act during the opponent's Focus. The harness should surface the (priorityHolder, focusHolder, state) triple at every window; any window where focus is null during a Showdown, or where the turn player silently keeps focus, is a bug.

title: Non-combat showdowns: opening, closing, and establishing control (341-348, 450-451, 466.5)
prompt: A Showdown opens when Control of a battlefield is Contested during a Cleanup and the turn is in a Neutral State (344), including the case where a unit moves to an EMPTY battlefield the mover does not control (450, 316.8.b.1.a — a stand-alone Non-Combat Showdown that is not a sub-phase of combat). Contrast three openings: (a) move into an empty uncontrolled battlefield — Non-Combat Showdown, no combat, mover establishes control at the close and Conquers (469.1); (b) move into a battlefield the opponent controls but has no units at — still a Non-Combat Showdown, defender may act on the chain to remove the mover; (c) move into a battlefield with opposing units — Combat staged, so the Showdown becomes the Combat Showdown Step (464.1-464.2), NOT a stand-alone showdown. Test 344.2: Contested applied with no opposing units present — what opens? Then closing (348): all players pass Focus without acting and the Showdown closes; for a Non-Combat Showdown do the 348.2 steps run (control established, Cleanup, scoring)? Yes/no contrasts a judge gets: the contester's only unit is killed on the chain during the Showdown — the Showdown must close without control changing and Contested must be removed at the next Cleanup (323.11); the DEFENDER kills the intruder with a Reaction and then the defender's own battlefield stays theirs but they do NOT re-score it if they already scored it this turn (470). Surface the Showdown open/close events, the focus holder at each pass, and the final controller plus points.

title: Trigger timing exotica and simultaneous-trigger ordering — new angle (382-385, 383.3.d, 319, 464.2)
prompt: Rounds 1, 2b, and 4 hammered simultaneous triggers, trigger costs at finalization, and triggers created during another effect's resolution, and they yielded many BUG facets — so re-probe from an angle those rounds did not take: triggers whose CONDITION is checked at a moment the engine may sample early or late. Test state-triggers versus event-triggers: 'while I am at a battlefield you control' style conditions evaluated during a Cleanup rather than when the event happened; a trigger whose condition became true and then false again before the Cleanup that would collect it (383 plus 319.7) — does it still trigger? Test a trigger that would fire during a Cleanup while another Cleanup is cascading (322) and assert it lands on the chain after the current Cleanup completes, not inside it (320). Test 'when this leaves the board' versus 'when this dies' for a unit that is Banished (427.2.a: Banish is not a subset of Kill) and for a unit Recalled (455-456: recalls are not moves, so move-triggers must not fire). Test a trigger on the OPPONENT's permanent that fires during the turn player's Cleanup — which seat is asked to order it, and does cross-player batching use turn order (383.3.d)? Finally: a trigger whose source leaves the board before the trigger resolves — the trigger still resolves and uses last-known information (359.3.e.13). Surface the batch composition and the seat asked to order each batch.

title: The three combat steps and damage assignment order (459-466, 465, 826)
prompt: Combat is staged during a Cleanup when opposing units share a battlefield (460-461) and then runs exactly three steps (463-466). Test staging first: 461.2 — a Combat that stops being staged before the steps begin is never resolved (kill the lone attacker with a Reaction and assert no damage step); 461.1 — with two battlefields both staging combat, who chooses which resolves first and is a Decision surfaced? Step 1 (464): the Combat Showdown, with the attacker→others→defender trigger order (464.2.e.1) and Reaction-timing spells legal for both seats. Step 2 (465): only if BOTH attacking and defending units remain; damage is ASSIGNED, and assignment is not Dealing (417.1.a) though it causes damage to be dealt — so 'when this deals damage' versus 'when this is dealt damage' must be distinguished. Assignment order is where Backline lives (826.3): a unit with Backline must be assigned lethal damage only after every other same-controller unit without Backline — contrast one Backline defender plus one vanilla defender (vanilla eats lethal first) against two Backline units (assigner chooses) and against a lone Backline unit (it takes it all). Also test that a Stunned unit contributes no might to damage but still must be assigned lethal equal to its FULL might (423.1.b-c), and that 465.3 skips FEPR and cancels outstanding tasks before the Resolution Step. Step 3 (466): combat cleanup, determine result, establish control (466.5), each with its own chain window. Surface the assignment Decision with the per-unit damage numbers.

title: Conquer versus Hold, once-per-battlefield-per-turn, and score triggers — new angle (467-471, 315.2.b)
prompt: Round 6 covered scoring edge cases, so come at 467-471 from the once-per-battlefield-per-turn bookkeeping angle (470) and from the trigger side (471.2). Contrasts: a player Conquers battlefield A during their own turn and then would Hold it during the SAME turn's Scoring Step — no second point; a player Conquers A on their turn and Conquers A again after losing and retaking it in the same turn — still no second point, and assert the per-battlefield-per-turn flag resets on the NEXT turn, not on control change; a player Conquers on the OPPONENT's turn (via a move granted at Reaction timing) — that is a Conquer, it scores, and it also consumes that battlefield's once-per-turn allowance for that player for that turn. Test 471.1: the point gain is 'up to one point' and 471.1.b caps a Conquer when the player is one point from the Victory Score — assert the exact point delta rather than assuming +1. Test 471.2: score triggers fire AT the battlefield that scored, so an ability reading 'when I conquer or hold' on a unit stationed at battlefield B must not fire when battlefield A scores; two score-triggered abilities at the same battlefield need an order Decision. Also test scoring while both battlefields hold simultaneously in the Scoring Step: two separate score events, two trigger batches, correct order. Surface each score event as (seat, battlefieldId, method, pointDelta) and the trigger order Decision.

title: Burn Out as a replacement effect and win-condition checks (431, 194, 323.1, 472)
prompt: Burn Out is defined as a Replacement Effect (431.5), not merely a state-based loss, and round 6 already found the engine declaring wins mid-resolution — re-probe the replacement framing. Test 431.1-431.2: a player must Burn Out when they would move one or more cards from an empty Main Deck; the sequence is shuffle the trash into the Main Deck and an opponent gains a point. Contrast the three ways to hit an empty deck: the mandatory Draw Phase draw (315.4.b.1, and the draw still completes afterward per 315.4.b.2), a card effect drawing 3 with only 1 left (413.4: draw as many as possible, burn out, then draw the remainder), and a Burn action (440) or Predict (436.4) hitting an empty deck — does the same replacement fire, and does Predict burn out at all? Test 431.3: an empty trash means the deck stays empty and Burn Out repeats; 431.3.c says points gained after the first Burn Out that cross the Victory Score win IMMEDIATELY rather than waiting for the Cleanup — contrast the FIRST burn-out point (which must wait for the next Cleanup per 323.1/472, so a resolving spell finishes all its instructions first) against a REPEATED burn-out point (immediate). Build the multi-card setup: a spell that draws 2 then creates a token, cast by a player with 1 card left and an empty trash, while the opponent sits at 7 points. Surface the win event's timing relative to the spell's remaining instructions and the chain contents at the moment the game ends.

title: Battlefields as objects: control, Contested status, and battlefield abilities (169-172, 188-193, 323.6-323.11)
prompt: Battlefields are game objects but NOT permanents (170-171), which changes what can touch them. Assert: battlefields can be targeted (170.7), can have passive, triggered, and activated abilities (170.8-170.10), cannot be killed or moved (170.3-170.4), and are locations (170.5) that hold any number of units (170.6). Control (190): established by having units at a battlefield at the end of a Showdown or Combat (190.4), it is a constant binary state (190.2/190.5), and crucially Control of a battlefield determines control of its ABILITIES (190.6) — build the judge's favorite setup: a battlefield with an activated ability, contested and then taken by the opponent mid-turn; the ability's controller flips, an already-finalized chain item created by the previous controller keeps its original controller (191.4), and the new controller may activate the ability only on their own turn (381). Test 323.6: in an Open State a player loses control of a battlefield with no units of theirs at it — but NOT during a Showdown/Closed state; contrast a unit recalled away during a Showdown against one recalled during the Main Phase. Test 323.11: Contested is removed from battlefields without units controlled by the player who applied it, and 323.11.a re-parks the surviving units. Also test 170.11 (battlefields referenced in different states in card text: controlled/uncontrolled/contested) and a battlefield TOKEN (187.8-187.9) entering play with abilities. Surface controller, contested flag, and staged showdown/combat per battlefield after each Cleanup.

title: The six steps of Play, choices at play versus resolution, and effect-plays versus hand-plays — new angle (349-359, 419.3)
prompt: Rounds 2b and 3 covered choices-at-play-vs-resolution and effect-plays versus hand plays, so re-probe the steps that neither round stressed: step 1 (354) and step 5 (358). 354.3-354.4: if another card effect is resolving or tasks are outstanding, the card sits on the chain and the process WAITS — build a play triggered mid-resolution of another spell and assert nothing finalizes until the outer effect finishes. 358 legality: 358.1 targets legal, 358.2 costs paid, 358.3 the outcome would not create an illegal state, 358.4 the timing permission exists, and 358.5 — if any check fails, everything done in the process is UNDONE and the action is cancelled; construct a failing case for each of the four checks and assert full rollback (resources restored, discarded cost cards back in hand, the card back in its origin zone), because partial rollback is the classic bug. 358.3.a is subtle: an effect preventing a game action does not prevent cards being PLAYED that would perform it. Also test 355.16 and 357.3 — a player may not make choices or pay costs that deterministically lead to an illegal state, so those options must be absent from the offered set rather than rejected after the fact. For the effect-play side, contrast 419.3.a-c: a play instructed by an effect is a Limited Action, follows all steps except as modified, and does NOTHING if no eligible card exists (no prompt at all). Surface the offered-choice sets and the pre/post state around each rollback.

title: What is and is not a target: the 355.9-355.13 taxonomy
prompt: This is the rules' own taxonomy and every clause deserves a pairing (355.6-355.13). 355.7: choosing specific objects makes them targets unless stated otherwise; 355.9: a valid target is on the board / on the chain / a player or zone, meets all targeting restrictions, and is never the spell itself (355.9.c — a 'counter a spell' spell cannot target itself). 355.9.a.1-a.5 fix defaults: 'unit', 'gear', 'rune' mean on the Board; 'spell' and 'ability' mean on the Chain; 'facedown card' means in a Facedown Zone; 'legend' means the Legend Zone; 'chosen champion' means the Champion Zone. 355.10 is the exclusion list that engines get wrong — an object mentioned in text is NOT targeted if it is in a non-Public zone (355.10.a; note Public zones are battlefields, bases, trashes, legend zones, champion zones, and facedown zones), if it appears only in another choice's restriction (355.10.b), if it appears only in a cost, trigger condition, or replacement effect including 'do X to do Y' costs (355.10.c), if it is programmatically selected by characteristics rather than chosen (355.10.d — and 355.10.d.2 says being the only valid choice does NOT make it programmatic), if it is part of a set chosen by other players (355.10.e), or if it is in a 'must' instruction (355.10.f). Build contrast pairs: 'kill a unit' (targets, so an untargetable unit is not offered) versus 'kill all units with 2 or less might' (no targets, so untargetable units still die); 'discard a card, then draw' (the discard is a cost, not a target). 355.12/355.13: 'may perform on some number' and 'any number' / 'up to' — assert 0 is a legal choice and that choosing 0 still puts the item on the chain. Surface the exact offered-target set for each variant.

title: Splitting damage among targets, and the resolution-time division (355.14)
prompt: Splitting has nine sub-rules and a genuinely two-phase decision structure (355.14). At FINALIZATION the targets are chosen (355.14.b) and their count may not exceed the total damage available (355.14.c); at RESOLUTION the division is decided (355.14.e) and each target must receive a valid amount, meaning a positive integer of at least 1 (355.14.f-g, 417.1.e). So a 'deal 3 damage split among any number of units' spell must offer 1, 2, or 3 targets but not 4, and must surface a SECOND Decision at resolution for the actual split — assert both Decisions exist and that the finalize-time prompt does not already ask for amounts. 355.14.d: each target is individually a target, so each triggers targeting-related effects (Deflect surcharges per target, 'when targeted' triggers per target, untargetable units excluded per target). 355.14.h is the judge question: if at resolution there are more targets than available damage — because damage was reduced or a target was removed — the player must still spread across as many targets as they have damage for and 355.14.h.1 forbids choosing fewer targets than damage. Build it: 3 damage split across 3 units, then a replacement reduces the total to 2 before resolution, or one target becomes illegal (359.3.e.5 — that target is unaffected and its damage is not redistributed... assert what the engine actually does versus 355.14.h). 355.14.i: costs paid or triggers fired from those objects being chosen still happened even if the object later becomes illegal. Surface the finalize-time target set and the resolution-time split Decision with per-target amounts.

title: Making new choices for a finalized chain item (750-755)
prompt: Some effects tell a player to make new choices for an item already finalized on the chain (750-755) and this is a rules area engines almost never implement fully. Assert the frame: it means the choices normally made during finalization, with exclusions (752 pointing back to 355); a player can choose any subset of the possible choices, including keeping some the same (753); if new choices make the item target something it did not previously target, that is a NEW targeting event so 'when targeted' triggers and Deflect-style surcharges apply to the newly chosen object (754); and any costs 'to play' incurred as a result of new choices must be paid (755) — construct exactly that: re-target a spell onto a Deflect unit (809) and assert the surcharge is demanded and that failure to pay unwinds correctly. Contrasts: re-choosing a mode on a modal spell (355.3) versus re-choosing a move destination (355.4) versus re-choosing a split (355.14 — can the split targets be re-picked, and does the damage cap re-apply?); re-choosing while the original target is now illegal; re-choosing an object whose choice was NOT a target (355.10) — is it even offered? Also test that re-choices cannot produce a deterministically illegal state (355.16) and that the item does not re-enter the pending state or re-open a priority window it already passed. The harness must surface a distinct 'new choices' Decision that lists the current choice alongside the alternatives; an engine that silently keeps the old choices or that re-runs the entire play process is wrong in different ways — record which.

title: Total cost determination order: base mods, additional, increases, discounts — new angle (356)
prompt: Round 2b covered costs under pressure; re-probe 356's ORDERING rules specifically, since the yield there was high. The order is fixed: base cost modifications (356.1), additional costs (356.2), increases (356.3), discounts (356.4), then total-cost modifications (356.5). Test 'play for [Cost]' replacing base costs (356.1.a) against 'ignoring its cost' zeroing base energy AND power (356.1.b.1) against 'ignoring its Energy cost' zeroing only energy (356.1.b.2) — and in every case assert 356.1.b.3: later additional costs and increases can still raise the total above zero. Test 356.2.a.2: the Deflect surcharge is a MANDATORY additional cost, so it is added at step 2 and can then be discounted at step 4; contrast with an optional additional cost like Accelerate (805.2) where 356.4.f.1 says it counts as 'paid' even if a discount reduced it to 0. Test 356.4.c-d ordering: component discounts apply when that component is added and must precede total-cost discounts; 356.4.e — a discount's minimum applies only to THAT discount, so a second discount may push below it; 356.6 — energy and power can never go below 0. Build the multi-card setup: a card with an optional additional cost, a domain power cost, one 'costs 1 less' effect with a minimum, one 'costs 1 less' without, and a Deflect target — then assert the exact final energy and per-domain power, and assert the payment prompt is asked once with the correct total rather than incrementally. Surface the computed cost breakdown per step.

title: Replacement effects on draw, damage, move, score, and channel events (367-375, 437, 438, 443)
prompt: Round 1 exhausted death-replacements; this theme deliberately avoids death and probes 367-375 on every OTHER event class. Draw: 'if you would draw, instead…' interacting with the mandatory Draw Phase draw (315.4.b) and with a multi-draw effect — is the replacement applied once per card drawn or once per draw INSTRUCTION (370.2: a replacement applies only once to an event or to the events that replace it)? Damage: Prevent is explicitly a delayed replacement effect (437.7); assert 437.2-437.4 — prevented damage is replaced by a reduced deal, the prevent value decrements, and a unit that had ALL its damage prevented was not dealt damage at all (so 'when I take damage' does not fire); contrast with combat assignment where damage is still assigned to a prevented unit (437.5). Move: a 'can't be moved' or redirect replacement versus a Recall, which 456.3 says cannot be blocked by movement restrictions. Score: a replacement on gaining points, checked against 471.1's 'up to one point'. Skip (443) is a replacement that replaces an event with nothing — apply it to a phase and to a trigger. Then the interaction rules: 372 (multiple replacements on the same event — the affected object's controller orders them), 373 (multiple simultaneous events — each is handled separately, controller assigns), 371 ('once each turn' replacements and 371.2.b's rule that a replacement not actually applied has not been used up), and 375 (an event modified by the very effect that generated it). Surface the ordering Decision, the applied-count per replacement, and the final event shape.

title: Activated ability process, timing, and location — new angle (376-381, 398-406)
prompt: Round 5 covered activated ability costs, targets, and timing broadly; re-probe the two constraints it did not isolate: 380 (abilities can primarily be activated only while on the Board) and 381 (all activated abilities can only be activated on the controlling player's turn, during an open state, unless a permissive keyword says otherwise). Build contrasts: a gear's activated ability while the gear is at a battlefield versus after it is recalled to base versus while it is in the trash or hand — only the board version should be offered; a battlefield's activated ability activated by the player who CONTROLS the battlefield (190.6), on their turn only, and the offered set flipping the instant control flips mid-turn; a legend's activated ability (174.8) which lives in the Legend Zone, not the board — does 380 permit it, and which seat may use it? Then Reaction-tagged abilities (813.2) that escape the closed-state restriction, and Add abilities with Reaction (429.3) that finalize and resolve immediately without passing priority, even during another player's priority window and even mid-payment (357.1.a). Test the negative: an Add ability WITHOUT Reaction used during the opponent's turn must be illegal; an Empower activation (827) that is legal only on your turn. Also 402-404: choices before costs, and an ability whose cost cannot be paid is never finalized. Surface the legal-action list per seat at each window and assert absence, not just rejection.

title: Reflexive triggers, delayed abilities, and linked abilities (386-397)
prompt: Three ability sub-kinds that engines usually collapse into inline resolution. Reflexive triggers (386-388): a 'then do this' clause creates a NEW chain item during resolution and uses the chain (388.1), so its choices are made when the reflexive item is finalized and both players get a priority window before it resolves — build a spell of the shape 'do X. Then, if X happened, do Y to a chosen target' and assert (a) a separate chain item appears, (b) the choice for Y is asked at that item's finalization not during the parent's resolution, and (c) the opponent may respond in between and can invalidate Y's target. Delayed abilities (389-392): they specify a window of applicability, are not associated with the unit or gear that created them (392), and survive their creator leaving the board — test 'at the end of this turn, recall that unit' where the source is killed first, and where the unit itself changes controller. Accelerate is a named delayed replacement (805.6), so use it as a second instance. Linked abilities (393-397): components must be printed in the same Effect Text and a component referencing an object affected by another component must resolve against THAT object (397) — build 'banish a card. Later, you may play the banished card' and test whether a second copy of the same card, or the same card banished by a different source, is wrongly playable (427.3.a says separate instances do not share). Surface each reflexive item as its own chain entry with its own Decision, and assert delayed abilities still fire after their source is gone.

title: Passive abilities on and off the board, and triggers in non-board zones (363-366, 384-385)
prompt: Passive abilities are the always-on layer (363-364), and the rules distinguish presence on permanents (365) from presence on cards OUTSIDE the board (366) — plus 384-385 do the same for triggered abilities, with 385.1 keying off the information level of the zone the card sits in. Test: a passive that says 'while I am in your trash, …' actually applying from the trash (a Public zone per 355.10.a.1) versus a passive on a card in HAND doing nothing unless its text explicitly grants a hand-zone function; a triggered ability on a card in hand (for example a Hidden-keyword prerequisite, 811.1.b) firing only where the zone's information level permits; a triggered ability on a card in the Champion Zone, which is Public (108.3.e). Contrast the same passive on a unit on the board (365) with the unit in the trash — does the engine keep the effect registered after the zone change, and does it correctly drop it when the object becomes a NEW object per 124? Test a passive that grants an ability to other objects and then leaves play mid-chain — the grant ends immediately, and any finalized chain item that depended on it does not un-finalize. Also test a battlefield's and a legend's passives (170.8, 174.6), which live on non-permanents and must not be swept by 'kill all permanents' or by board-clear logic. Surface the active-passive registry per zone and assert entries appear and disappear at the right zone transitions.

title: Deck manipulation: Draw, Recycle, Burn, Predict, and simultaneous ordering (413, 416, 436, 440)
prompt: Four deck actions with sharp per-action rules. Draw (413.1.a default from the top; 413.4 on an empty deck). Recycle (416): main deck cards go to the Main Deck, runes to the Rune Deck (416.1.a-b), EACH player recycles to their own decks regardless of who controls the effect (416.1.c) — build a 'each player recycles 2 from their trash' effect with cards owned by the other player in a trash and assert ownership routing (056: cards a player owns may never be placed in another player's non-board zone). 416.5 is the testable ordering rule: 2 or more cards recycled simultaneously go to the BOTTOM in an order chosen by the recycling player — assert a Decision offering the order, then assert the resulting deck order by drawing them back. 416.3-416.4: recycle as a cost must be completable, and as an effect you must recycle as many as possible. Burn (440): top of Main Deck to trash, as many as possible (440.4) — contrast with Discard (422, from hand) and assert 'when I am discarded' triggers do NOT fire on a burn. Predict (436): look at the top card and choose to keep or move it; 436.4 caps it at the available cards. Then the interactions a judge is asked: Predict then Draw (do you get the card you just predicted?), Recycle-to-bottom then Burn (which card burns?), and any of these with an empty deck triggering Burn Out (431). Surface the ordering Decisions and the resulting top-N deck contents.

title: State actions: Exhaust, Ready, Stun, Empower/Disempower (414, 415, 423, 441-442, 827-828)
prompt: Four binary states with idempotence rules that engines get subtly wrong. Exhaust (414.1.b-c): an already-exhausted object cannot be exhausted again and nothing additional happens — so 'exhaust an enemy unit' targeting an exhausted unit is legal but does nothing, while 'exhaust me' as a COST (414.4) fails outright if already exhausted and therefore the ability must not be offered. Ready (415.1.b-c) mirrors this. Stun (423): binary (423.1.a), a stunned unit cannot be stunned again (423.1.a.1 — build the 'when you stun a unit' trigger and assert it does NOT fire on re-stunning an already-stunned unit), stunned units lose the status at expiration step 3d (423.1.a.2), contribute no might in the damage step but still soak lethal equal to their FULL might (423.1.b-c). Empower (441)/Disempower (442) plus the Empower keyword (827) and the Empowered dependent keyword (828): activating Empower makes the source Empowered (827.2), multiple Empower instances are separate activated abilities (827.3), and an Empowered-dependent ability turns on only while the state holds — test disempowering in response to an activation that already finalized (the ability still resolves) versus before it is activated (the ability is not offered). Cross-pairings: stun a unit then buff it and check combat damage; exhaust a unit as the Standard Move cost (420.3.a) and assert it cannot then pay a second exhaust cost. Surface per-unit (ready/exhausted, stunned, empowered) after each step.

title: Countering, what a countered card did and did not do, and 'can't be countered' (425, 054, 419.4)
prompt: Countering (425) has four consequences that must be tested separately. 425.1.a: a countered card or ability does nothing and is cleared from the chain, and 425.1.a.1 sends the card to the trash — so assert the card is in the TRASH, not banished or back in hand. 425.1.b: a countered card is NOT considered played for abilities that trigger on cards being played — but 419.4.a.1 says the act of playing already COMPLETED before resolution, so 'when you play a spell' triggers that already fired stay fired while 'when a spell resolves' does not; build a Legion-style dependent keyword (812) satisfied by playing a card and assert whether countering the card un-satisfies Legion. 425.1.c-c.1: countering refunds nothing, including additional costs — assert the resources and any discarded/killed cost objects stay spent. Then 'can't be countered': 054 (can't beats can) plus 358.3 legality — a counter spell targeting an uncounterable spell must NOT be offered that target at all rather than fizzling later, and if the uncounterable status is GAINED after the counter is finalized, the counter resolves and does nothing while the target survives (359.3.e.5). Also test countering an ABILITY on the chain (425.3 covers abilities), including a triggered ability whose source is already dead, and countering a reflexive trigger item (388.1). Multi-card judge setup: two counters on the chain aimed at each other. Surface the offered counter-target set and the post-resolution zone of every object involved.

title: Kill versus Banish, active versus passive kills, and kill attribution (427, 428)
prompt: 428.5 is an attribution system that 'killed by' cards depend on. Test active kill (428.1.a.1 — a kill instruction or a kill paid as a cost) versus passive kill (428.1.a.2 — lethal damage or a consequence), and assert both route through the trash from the board (428.2) and that only board origins count as Killed (428.2.a). 428.1.a.1.b: a unit with Deathknell killed by a kill instruction still gets its trigger collected. Attribution contrasts a judge is asked: a spell containing a kill instruction is responsible (428.5.b); units killed by a Cleanup are attributed to the spell/ability whose damage caused it and the responsible player is the one responsible for the deal action (428.5.c-c.1); combat-cleanup deaths are attributed to the combat damage sources (428.5.c.2); and abilities attributed a kill are attributed IN ADDITION to their source (428.5.d). Build a card that cares about 'a unit killed by a spell this turn' and drive it three ways — direct kill instruction, lethal damage from a spell resolving into a Cleanup, and combat damage — and assert which of the three satisfy it. Then Banish (427): it is neither a Kill nor a Discard (427.2.a-b), it moves the card directly to Banishment from any origin, and separate instances of the same-named object do not share banished-card memory (427.3.a) — so 'play the card banished by this' with two copies of the source must not cross-wire. Also assert a banished TOKEN ceases to exist (186.1, 438.6). Surface the killedBy attribution list per death.

title: Buff counters, the one-buff cap, and counters generally (426, 701-711, 742-749)
prompt: The Buff action has a cap that is easy to implement wrong (426.1.b.1): if a unit already has a Buff counter, buffing it again does NOTHING — but 426.1.c says such a unit can still be CHOSEN for a buff effect, it simply is not buffed, so targeting and 'when targeted' triggers still fire while the might does not change. 426.1.b.2: some effects explicitly grant permission to be buffed multiple times and ignore the cap — test one buffed unit hit by a normal buff (no change) and by a permission-granting buff (stacks), and a unit with TWO permission sources. 703: each buff contributes +1 might; 705: a unit leaving play loses all buffs, and 705.1 adds that Champions do not retain buffs in the Champion Zone even if they return there — build the champion round-trip and assert the buff is gone on the return. Then the general counter rules (742-749): counters are game objects on the board that can be referenced, counted, spent (745), moved between objects where the counter is on exactly one at a time (746), cease to exist if removed without a new host (747), and are lost entirely when the object changes zones to a non-board zone (748, cross-check 124's new-object rule). Test a 'move a counter from one unit to another' effect where the destination is illegal at resolution, and an effect that counts counters mid-resolution after some were spent as a cost. Surface per-unit counter inventories and the might arithmetic that follows.

title: Create, Replace-and-swap-back, Swap, and Double (432, 433, 438, 439)
prompt: Four rarely-tested actions with precise definitions. Create (439): produces an object that did not exist, at a directed destination (439.2), in a specified state (439.3), defaulting per 439.4 — test a token created READY versus the default, and created at a battlefield the creator does not control (184.2 restricts where a token may be played). Replace (438): create a token in the place of another card or token WITHOUT playing it (438.1); the replaced card goes to BANISHMENT (438.5), not the trash, and it is explicitly not a subset of Banishing for trigger purposes (438.4); a replaced TOKEN stops existing once it reaches banishment (438.6); and 438.7 allows a swap-back — the created token is exchanged for the original, which round 6 already found broken for facedown-carrying battlefields, so probe swap-back for UNITS instead: does the returning card come back with damage, buffs, attachments, and location intact, and where do attached gear go? Swap (433): increase one numeric value and decrease another on the same or different objects — test a swap that would push a value below zero and one that hits a floor. Double (432): increase a numeric attribute by its CURRENT value, so doubling 0 is still 0 and doubling after a buff uses the post-buff number — build a might-doubling effect with a this-turn pump on the chain above it and assert LIFO order changes the result. Surface the created object's full characteristics (187) and the pre/post numbers for each swap and double.

title: Attach/Detach and top-most cards beyond Equipment — new angle (434-435, 716-719, 724)
prompt: Round 3 covered Equipment effect text and holders; re-probe the generic attachment machinery (716-719) with NON-Equipment attachments and with stacks deeper than one. 717-718: attaching links cards to combine effects, and Attached is a state; 719 defines the Top-Most Card as the one with cards linked to it. 434.4: an attached card's location becomes the top-most card's location, and 435.4: on detach its location is the one the top-most card was at — so build a gear attached to a unit that then MOVES to a battlefield, is RECALLED to base (455, 457, 323.7), and finally is killed, and assert the attachment's location and zone at each step, including who owns/controls the detached gear. 434.5: attaching does not change either card's state — so an exhausted attacher stays exhausted and attaching does not ready or exhaust the host. 434.3/435.3: attach and detach do not inherently target, but effects that attach may — test an attach effect against an untargetable host (757-758) and assert whether it is offered. Then the Inactive rule that gives attachments meaning: 724 says Effect Text is Inactive unless the card is Attached, and 723 says Rules Text is never Inactive by default — so a gear's Rules Text works at base while its Effect Text only works while attached; test a two-card stack where the middle card's Effect Text grants something to the top-most card, and detaching the bottom one. Surface the attachment tree, per-card active/inactive text, and locations.

title: Deal, Heal, sources of damage, and Bonus Damage stacking — new angle (417, 418, 712-715)
prompt: Round 3 covered damage modifiers on every path; re-probe the SOURCE-attribution half of 417.6, which round 3 did not isolate. 417.6.a: an effect that does not specify a source is itself the source; 417.6.b: an effect that names a source makes that object the origin; 417.6.b.2.a: when an ABILITY is the source, it is in addition to the spell or unit it lives on; 417.6.b.3: a spell that names a unit as the damage source makes the UNIT the source; 417.6.b.4: the source's controller is responsible for the deal action; 417.6.c-c.1: combat damage has the opposing units as its sources. Build a card that cares about 'damage dealt by a unit you control' and drive it four ways — a spell dealing damage directly, a spell dealing damage 'as though from' a unit, a unit's activated ability dealing damage, and combat damage — asserting which satisfy the condition and which seat is credited. Then 712-715 Bonus Damage: it is a property granted to a Deal ACTION (713), multiple instances all apply (714), and it applies to the TOTAL damage of one instance (715), not per target — so a split-damage spell (355.14) with +1 Bonus Damage must gain 1 total, not 1 per target; assert the exact number. 417.1.e-e.1: only valid (>=1) damage is dealt, so a 0-damage deal does not fire 'when I take damage'. Heal (418): clearing damage for any reason is Healing (418.1.a), so a replacement that removes damage counts and 'when a unit is healed' triggers fire. Surface source attribution and per-unit damage marks.

title: Runes, rune pools, Add/Pay, floating resources, and restricted power (160-168, 429, 444, 167)
prompt: The resource system is a whole subsystem and deserves its own theme. Structure: runes are not Main Deck cards (161.1), live in the Rune Deck (161.2), produce Energy for numeric costs and Power for domain-associated costs (163.1-163.2), and the six basic runes each carry two abilities (164.2). Pools: resources must be Added to the pool before they can be spent (166.2), and every player's pool empties at the START of each player's Main Phase and the END of each turn (167, 316.3, 317.2.d) — so build a player who Adds during the opponent's turn at Reaction timing and assert the float survives until the correct emptying point, and that floating across the opponent's ENTIRE turn into your own Main Phase does NOT survive. Add (429): triggered and activated Add abilities resolve as soon as they are finalized and do NOT pass priority (429.2-429.2.a), while a SPELL that Adds lingers on the chain normally (429.2.b) — assert the opponent gets a window for the spell and none for the ability. 429.3: a Reaction-tagged Add ability may be activated any time you could pay, finalizing and resolving immediately even mid-payment (357.1.a) — build a payment that is only affordable if the player taps a rune during step 4 and assert the harness surfaces that opportunity. Pay (444): removing from the pool, with domain matching — test paying a two-domain power cost from a pool that has the pips in the wrong domains, a rainbow/any-domain source, and an over-payment attempt. Also Recycle of runes to the Rune Deck (416.1.b). Surface the pool as (energy, per-domain power) before and after every step.

title: Standard Move, multi-unit moves, forced moves, and move legality (144, 420, 445-453)
prompt: Movement has both a discretionary and a limited form and they behave differently (420.2-420.3). Standard Move (144, 420.3): the cost is exhausting one or more units and the effect is moving them — so test a multi-unit standard move where all movers exhaust and all arrive simultaneously (one Contested application, one Showdown, one Cleanup per 453), versus moving them one at a time (two Cleanups, possibly two showdowns). Assert an already-exhausted unit cannot be part of the cost (414.1.b) and that the move is not offered for it. Forced/effect moves (420.2, 449): a spell that moves an ENEMY unit — who chooses the destination, and when? 355.4 says the destination is chosen at finalization, and 355.4.a says it must be a location other than the unit's current one where it is allowed to be — assert the destination Decision appears BEFORE the opponent's response window, and that an enemy unit forced into your battlefield applies Contested per 450 with the MOVER's controller as the contester (345 gives them Focus). Test destination legality: a battlefield the moving unit's controller does not control is valid for a move but not for a PLAY (355.2.a), base-to-base moves, and 'move here' effects where the source location equals the destination (illegal). Test that a move completing performs a Cleanup (453) and that a move into an empty enemy-controlled battlefield stages a Non-Combat Showdown (451, 316.8.b.1). Surface the mover set, destination Decision, contested flags, and the post-move Cleanup log.

title: Recalls are not moves: triggers, restrictions, state, and gear (454-458, 323.7)
prompt: A Recall relocates a permanent from anywhere to its Base without being a Move (455-456) and the distinction drives four testable consequences. 456.1: move-triggered abilities do NOT fire on a recall — build a 'when a unit moves' watcher on each side and assert silence on recall but firing on a standard move to base if such a move exists. 456.2: a recall still changes location, so 'while I am at a battlefield' passives switch off and location-based targeting changes. 456.3: a recall CANNOT be blocked by effects that restrict or block movement — build a 'units can't move' or 'this unit can't leave' effect and assert the recall still happens (054's can't-beats-can applies to the move restriction, not to the recall). 458/458.1: recalls do not affect state, so damage, exhaustion, stun, buffs, and counters all persist through the recall — assert each one explicitly, including that a recalled unit stays exhausted rather than readying. Then the automatic recalls in the Cleanup (323.7): unattached non-unit gear and non-unit runes at battlefields, and all permanents and runes in battlefield zones that no longer exist, are recalled — build the gear case (457.1) and a battlefield that leaves play with objects on it. Finally, contrast recall with 'return to hand' (a zone change to a non-board zone, so 124 makes it a new object, buffs and counters are lost per 705/748) — the two must not share an implementation. Surface location, state flags, and trigger log per operation.

title: Layer order, dependency, timestamps, and might floors (473-480, 701-711)
prompt: The layer system (473-480) is applied repeatedly until stable (476, 476.2), in the order trait-altering, ability-altering, arithmetic (477.1-477.3), with copy effects in layer 1 (477.1.b) and keyword grants in layer 2 (477.2.a). Build cases where the order is observable: an effect that makes a unit into a copy of another (layer 1) plus an effect granting it a keyword (layer 2) plus a +2 might pump (layer 3) — assert the final characteristics and that the pump survives the copy rather than being erased. Dependency (478-479): when two same-layer effects alter each other's application, the dependent one applies later; 479.1 says mutual alteration establishes NO dependency, so timestamps decide (480). Timestamps: 480.1 an effect stamps when it begins applying; 480.2 rules text that becomes Inactive LOSES its timestamp and gets a new one when it becomes active again — build an Equipment whose Effect Text goes inactive on detach and active again on re-attach, and assert its grant now applies AFTER an effect that was previously later. Then arithmetic and might floors: 477.3.b limits arithmetic effects from non-passive sources; assert might can never be driven below its floor by stacked debuffs and that Mighty (706-711) is evaluated on CURRENT might on the board (710) but PRINTED might off the board (711) — so a buffed 4-might unit is Mighty on the board and not Mighty once it is in hand or trash. Surface the layer-by-layer computed characteristics for one unit and the timestamps involved.

title: Copies and 'becomes a copy of' (124, 206, 477.1.b, 187)
prompt: Copying is layer-1 (477.1.b) and copies PRINTED or copied values only. Test: a unit that becomes a copy of another unit takes its name, might, tags, keywords, and abilities, but not its damage, buffs, counters, exhaustion, location, or attachments; a copy of a unit that is itself already a copy copies the copied values (206 says cost lookups always use the printed or copied cost); a token copying a card (185: tokens are not cards, so 'card' effects still do not see it, per 052's rule that 'card' means Main Deck card). Contrast with a token CREATED as a duplicate (439, 187) versus an existing permanent BECOMING a copy — the first is a new object entering the board (359.2.c enters exhausted for units) and the second keeps its zone, location, and state. Test the interaction judges ask about: copy a unit, then the original leaves play — the copy is unaffected because copies do not track the source; copy a unit that is currently buffed — the copy gets the printed might, not the buffed might; copy a unit with an Equipment attached — the Equipment's granted text is NOT copied because it comes from another card, not the printed text. Also test 124: an object changing zones to or from a non-board zone becomes a NEW object, so 'becomes a copy' ends when the copy is recalled to hand and replayed. Surface the copy's full characteristic set alongside the source's and assert every field individually rather than in aggregate.

title: Inactive text, ignored abilities, and dependent keywords (720-727, 765-767, 824, 828)
prompt: Text can be present but not doing anything, and the rules distinguish two separate mechanisms. Inactive (720-725): inactive text is still PRESENT on the card (722) so it can be referenced and counted; Rules Text is never Inactive by default (723) while Effect Text is Inactive unless the card is Attached (724); 725 allows partial re-activation. Ignored (765-767): an effect may instruct a player to ignore abilities while performing a specific game action, those abilities are treated as inactive only for that action or procedure (766-767), and they resume immediately afterward — build 'do X ignoring abilities' where the ignored ability would otherwise trigger, and assert the trigger neither fires during the action nor fires retroactively afterward. Dependent keywords (726-727): Legion (812), Level (824), and Empowered (828) are only active while their condition holds; 824.1.c says a Level ability is active as long as the controlling player has N XP — so test crossing the XP threshold mid-chain (does an already-finalized item keep the Level text?) and dropping below it. 480.2 links the two areas: inactive text loses its timestamp, so re-activation re-orders it against other effects — assert that. Also test whether an inactive ability is still a referenceable characteristic (805.5, 807.3, etc. — 'whether or not a card has X' is checkable), so a card asking 'does this unit have Assault' should still see printed-but-inactive text. Surface a per-card text-state map (active / inactive / ignored) at each step.

title: Token creation, characteristics, and ceasing to exist (179-187)
prompt: Tokens have their own object rules that engines routinely fold into cards. 182-183: a token's controller is the controller of the creating spell or ability unless specified, and its owner is the player who controlled that effect — so a token created by YOUR spell at the opponent's location is still yours; build a control-change effect on a token and assert owner versus controller separately. 185/185.1-185.3: tokens are NOT cards, so effects that say 'card' (52: shorthand for Main Deck card) must not see them — test 'discard a card', 'recycle a card', 'return a card to hand' against a token. 186/186.1 is the big one: tokens exist only on the board or the chain, and a token put into any non-board zone besides the chain CEASES TO EXIST immediately after — so a killed token is not in the trash (round 2 already found this broken for a Gold token, so test other token classes here: a Recruit unit token, a Sand Soldier, a Mech, a Bird with Deflect, a Tentacle, a Reflection, a Shadow Clone, per 187.1-187.11), a bounced token vanishes from hand, a banished token vanishes (438.6). Assert the downstream consequence: a 'when a unit dies' trigger still fires for the token's death, but a later 'return a unit from your trash' cannot find it, and trash-count effects do not see it. 184: creation may specify ready/exhausted state, restricted location, and temporary grants; 187.8-187.9 cover BATTLEFIELD tokens, which are locations with abilities. Surface each token's (owner, controller, zone, exists) after every step.

title: Legends, the Champion Zone, Signature cards, XP, and Level (173-176, 108.3, 103.2, 728-733, 824)
prompt: Legends and the Chosen Champion sit outside the normal permanent lifecycle. Legends (174-176): owned, never shuffled, cannot be killed or moved (174.3-174.4), CAN be targeted (174.5), and can carry passive, triggered, and activated abilities (174.6-174.8) — so test 'kill a permanent' and 'move a unit' offered against a legend (they must not be), 'ready a legend' which DOES target because the Legend Zone is Public (355.10.a), and a legend's activated ability's timing (381). Champion Zone (108.3): the Chosen Champion starts there, cannot be RETURNED there by normal means (108.3.c), can be played from there as a normal play (108.3.d, 419.1.a), and is Public information (108.3.e) — build the judge sequence: play the champion, it dies to the trash, is returned to hand, is played again from hand; assert it never re-enters the Champion Zone, and assert 705.1 (a champion loses buffs in the Champion Zone). Signature and Champion tags (133.7.a-b, 133.8.b, 103.2.d): deck-construction supertypes that cards may also reference in play — test a card that checks 'a Signature card' or the Champion tag. XP (728-733): a resource that is not a game object (731), unlimited (733), not shared between allies (732), gained and spent (730) — test spending XP as a cost that cannot be paid, and Level (824) turning a dependent ability on and off as XP crosses N, including mid-chain. Surface XP totals per seat, the champion's zone history, and the legend's offered-action list.

title: Combat keyword cluster: Assault, Shield, Tank, Backline (807, 814, 815, 826)
prompt: One cluster, four keywords, all interacting in the Combat Damage Step (465). Assault (807): a passive; if a unit has or is granted Assault and is granted it again, the values of all granted instances combine per 807.2 — test printed Assault 2 plus granted Assault 1 and assert the total, and assert the keyword is a referenceable characteristic (807.3) even when the unit is not in combat. Shield (814.2) and Deflect (809.2) use the same 'values of all granted instances' wording — test Shield 1 printed plus Shield 2 granted, and whether shield is consumed per damage instance or per combat. Tank (815): multiple instances are redundant (815.2) — assert a second Tank grant changes nothing, and test what Tank forces in damage assignment against Backline on the same side. Backline (826.3): functionally 'I must be assigned lethal damage after any other unit with the same controller that does not have Backline', and it alters how the assigning player may ELECT to assign (826.4) — build the four-unit board (attacker with 5 might; defenders: one Tank, one vanilla, one Backline) and assert the legal assignment orderings offered, then the illegal one rejected. Cross-pairings: a Stunned Tank (423.1.b-c contributes no might but still soaks full-might lethal), a Backline unit that is the ONLY unit left, and Assault on a unit that never actually enters combat. Surface the damage-assignment Decision with each unit's required minimum and the final damage marks.

title: Deflect, Ganking, and Hunt (809, 810, 823)
prompt: Three keywords that modify what the opponent may do to or with a unit. Deflect (809): a passive that imposes a MANDATORY additional cost on spells and abilities that target the object (356.2.a.2) — test that the surcharge is added at step 2 of cost determination and can therefore be discounted (356.4.f), that it is charged once per targeting of that object (and per target on a multi-target or split spell, 355.14.d), that it is charged when a NEW choice re-targets onto the Deflect unit (754-755), and that a player who cannot pay simply is not offered the target (355.16, 358.5). 809.2: multiple granted Deflect values combine. Ganking (810): a passive, multiple instances redundant (810.2) — test what it permits about moving into a contested or defended battlefield and contrast a unit with Ganking against the same unit without, including whether the mover joins an in-progress combat or opens a new showdown (316.8, 461). Hunt (823): a triggered keyword whose values combine when granted multiple times (823.2) — test the trigger condition firing exactly once per qualifying event, the value arithmetic with two grants, and the case where the trigger's target is gone at resolution (359.3.e). Judge setup for the cluster: a Ganking unit moving into a battlefield defended by a Deflect unit, while the mover has Hunt — assert the ordering of the move's Cleanup, the Hunt trigger, and the opponent's response window, and that a removal spell aimed at the Deflect defender costs the surcharge even at Reaction timing during the showdown.

title: Legion, Accelerate, Flow, Repeat (812, 805, 829, 820)
prompt: Four keywords about how and when a card gets played. Legion (812) is a dependent keyword: ALL instances of Legion on cards a player controls are satisfied by that player playing a SINGLE card (812.2) — so build a board with three Legion sources and assert one card play turns them all on, then assert the timing question: does playing the Legion card itself satisfy Legion for that same card, and does a COUNTERED card still satisfy it (425.1.b versus 419.4.a — construct both readings and pick the rules-correct one). Accelerate (805): an optional additional cost paid as you play the unit (805.2), no function on the board (805.3), redundant if duplicated (805.4), and it generates a DELAYED replacement effect that replaces entering exhausted with entering ready (805.6) — test paying Accelerate on a non-hand play (from trash or from banishment), test a discount reducing the Accelerate cost to 0 while it still counts as paid (356.4.f.1), and test a second effect that also makes the unit enter ready (370.2: a replacement applies only once). Flow (829): a passive on spells — probe its play-from-trash permission and whether it is respected for a spell moved to the trash mid-turn versus one that was already there. Repeat (820): an optional additional cost that runs the instructions an additional time, with choices made at the usual time (820.2) and multiple instances paid separately (820.3) — test a Repeat on a targeted spell (are targets re-chosen or reused?) and a Repeat where the second execution's targets are all illegal.

title: Deathknell, Temporary, Mighty, Empower/Empowered (808, 816, 706-711, 827-828)
prompt: A cluster around leaving play and around threshold-dependent state. Deathknell (808): each instance triggers separately (808.2), it is collected at Cleanup step 3a before the kill at 3b (323.4-323.5), and it survives a kill-as-cost (428.1.a.1.b) — test a unit with TWO Deathknells (two triggers, order chosen by controller), a Deathknell unit banished instead of killed (427.2.a: no trigger), and a Deathknell unit that ceases to exist as a token (186.1 — does the trigger still resolve?). Temporary (816): a triggered keyword, redundant if duplicated (816.2), that kills the permanent at the appropriate expiration timing — test its interaction with the Expiration Step's fixed order (317.2.b-d: heal precedes 'this turn' expiry) and with the 317.2.f re-loop when its death creates further triggers. Mighty (706-711): 'is Mighty' means might 5 or greater (708) and 'becomes Mighty' fires at the moment might crosses from below 5 to 5 or more (709) — build a unit at 4 might, buff it to 5 (becomes Mighty fires), debuff to 4 and re-buff to 5 (fires again?), and a unit printed at 5 entering play (is that a 'becomes'?); assert board-current versus non-board-printed evaluation (710-711). Empower/Empowered (827-828): activating Empower makes the source Empowered (827.2) and multiple Empower abilities are separately activatable (827.3); an Empowered-dependent ability is live only while the state holds (828.1) — test disempowering (442) after an Empowered ability is finalized. Surface the trigger batches and the might timeline.

title: Timing keywords: Ambush, Action, Reaction, and Hidden's granted Reaction (822, 806, 813, 811.6)
prompt: Permissive keywords decide WHEN a card may be played, and the rules are explicit that they change nothing else. Action (806): permission not restricted to showdowns, inclusive of all other timings (806.2), and it never alters the card's instructions (806.3); a passive may GRANT Action, in which case the card does not have the keyword but has the permission (806.4) — test the difference by asking a card that checks 'does this have Action' (806.5). Reaction (813): permission escaping closed states and showdowns (813.2), same grant-versus-have distinction (813.4-813.5); test a Reaction spell played during the opponent's turn, during a combat showdown, and in response to a finalized chain item, versus the same spell without Reaction, and assert seat.can is false in the second case rather than the play failing later (358.4). Ambush (822): a passive with a location choice that becomes invalid if there are no units at the chosen location before finalization completes (822.3) — build the race where the last unit at that location dies while the Ambush unit is pending, and assert the location choice is re-asked or the play rolls back (358.5). Hidden (811.6): a card that is Hidden GAINS Reaction while facedown or when played from facedown, so it may be played at any Reaction timing — contrast playing the same card from hand (normal timing per 811.3, no Reaction) with playing it from a facedown zone (Reaction timing) and assert the legal-window difference. Surface the per-seat legal-play list at each of four windows: your main phase, opponent's main phase, a non-combat showdown, and the combat showdown step.

title: Reveal, Hide, privacy levels, and what each seat may know — new angle (421, 424, 128, 109)
prompt: Round 6 covered the hidden/facedown lifecycle; re-probe the INFORMATION rules themselves. 128.3-128.5 define Secret (no player may look), Private (only the controller/owner), and Public (any player) — and 109 says everything in the collective play areas is public information, which 128 then qualifies. Assert per-zone privacy: hand is private, main deck is secret, trash and base and battlefields and legend and champion zones are public (355.10.a.1 lists the public set, and note Facedown Zones are listed as PUBLIC zones for targeting even though the card faces are secret — test exactly that split: a facedown card is a legal target for 'a facedown card' effects while its face stays unknown). Reveal (424): revealing presents a card from a zone others cannot see, it is a temporary state and not a zone (424.1.a), the card STAYS in its zone (424.1.a.2), the state lasts as long as the effect says (424.1.a.3), revealed cards can be further manipulated while revealed (424.4.a), and 424.3.a covers revealing a whole zone with later additions not automatically revealed — build 'reveal your hand until end of turn' then draw a card and assert the new card is not revealed. 421.4: a facedown card that would change zones, or when the game ends, is revealed to all players — test both. Then the harness-visibility assertion that matters most: for every Decision surfaced, assert the option list given to seat A never leaks the face of a secret or private card belonging to seat B, and that a 'choose a card at random from opponent's hand' effect is implemented without exposing the hand.

title: 'Can't beats can', do-as-much-as-you-can, and untargetable restrictions (054-056, 757-758, 358.3)
prompt: The Golden and Silver rules are testable invariants, not flavor. 054: can't beats can — build direct collisions and assert the restriction wins every time: 'units can't be killed' versus a kill instruction; 'you can't draw cards' versus a draw effect (and then versus the mandatory Draw Phase draw, 315.4.b, which must be skipped rather than crashing, and check whether Burn Out is thereby avoided); 'this can't be moved' versus a forced move (and then versus a Recall, which 456.3 says is unstoppable by movement restrictions — the recall still happens, so the restriction does NOT win there because it is not a move). 055: do as much as you can, ignoring impossible instructions — build a multi-instruction spell where instruction 2 is impossible and assert 1 and 3 still execute (359.3.e.6, 359.3.e.11 partial execution). 056: cards a player owns may never be placed into another player's non-board zone — build 'return target unit to its owner's hand' on a unit you control but do not own, and a discard/recycle effect that would route an owned card to the wrong trash or deck (416.1.c). 757-758: 'can't be chosen by' makes an object an illegal target for the indicated set, so it must be ABSENT from the offered set, while effects that do not choose (355.10.d) still hit it — build the pair. 358.3: a play whose outcome would create an illegal state fails legality and fully unwinds. Surface, for each collision, the offered-action set (absence, not rejection) and the post-state proving the restriction held.

title: Concede, player removal, and end-of-game invariants (649-652, 194-196, 421.4)
prompt: Conceding is legal at any time (650) and removes the player from the game in progress (651), with 652's removal steps applying if the game continues. In a 2-player engine, concede must end the game immediately with the opponent as the winner (195: a player wins if they are the only one left) — test conceding at every awkward moment: with items on the chain mid-FEPR, during a Cleanup, during the Combat Damage Step, while a Decision is pending for the OTHER seat, and while the conceding player has already reached the Victory Score. Assert the game-over state is terminal: no further Decisions are surfaced, no triggers resolve, the chain is not drained, and the harness reports a single winner. 196: when a player wins, the game ends — so build the race where a Cleanup would both hand player A the Victory Score and kill player B's last unit, and assert nothing after the win executes (round 6 already found the engine executing instructions after a win, so this is a follow-up from the concede side). 421.4: when the game ends, facedown cards are revealed to all players — assert the final state exposes them. Also probe the invariants a headless harness must hold with no undo: every rejected action leaves state byte-identical to before (358.5 full rollback), and replaying the same seed and the same decision sequence reproduces the identical final state — build one long scenario, snapshot, attempt several illegal actions, and assert the snapshot is unchanged.

title: Controller versus owner across every zone change — new angle (188-193, 056, 124)
prompt: Rounds 1 and 5 covered controller-versus-owner for possession, recall, and activation; re-probe the ROUTING half — where an object physically goes when a borrowed object leaves the board. 056 is absolute: cards a player owns may never be placed into a non-board zone belonging to another player, and 056.1 enumerates those zones (main deck, rune deck, trash, hand, champion zone). So for a unit you control but do not own, test every exit: killed (owner's trash), banished (whose banishment?), returned to hand (owner's hand), recycled (owner's deck, 416.1.c), discarded as a cost by the controller (still the owner's trash), and replaced (438.5 banishment). Then the reverse question for tokens (183: owner is the player who controlled the creating effect) and for a token whose control was taken — it still ceases to exist per 186.1 rather than landing in anyone's trash. 191.3: a permanent entering the board assigns control to the player who brought it in — so a unit played from the OPPONENT's trash by your effect is controlled by you and owned by them; assert both, then kill it and assert the routing. 124: leaving to a non-board zone makes it a NEW object, so control grants, damage, buffs, and counters all end. Also assert 192: 'controller' references resolve to the current controller at the moment of the check, not at the time the effect was created, while an already-finalized chain item keeps its original controller (191.4). Surface (owner, controller, zone) triples after each transition.
